title: E44 - Building a Law Firm and a Product: LawPro.ai Co-Founder and Zirkin Schmerling Partner, Josh Schmerling
author: Josh Schmerling

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source contains only podcast closing remarks and provides no substantive claims, evidence or argument bearing on the cluster’s proposition that legal-AI optimism should remain conditional, user-led and attentive to verification, workflow readiness and distinct market scenarios.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source discusses possible technology-driven changes in personal-injury demand and specialist referrals, but does not address whether human oversight provides effective control, requires independent verification, preserves expertise, or is adequately governed by professional rules.
qs: And I'm sure like you guys have got to be thinking like, you know, the data suggests that full self-driving cars get into way less accidents, and we could see like a like a massive drop in that.

I think there was a article put out, or some kind of a paper put up by one of the insurance companies, it might have been Geico, saying that they thought that basically car accidents were going to primarily come to an end in the next 10 years.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source does not address access to justice or whether AI uptake can close justice gaps. It does, however, align with the cluster’s narrower distinction between widespread experimentation and deeper organizational adoption: reported use is high, while Schmerling characterizes investment and maturity as still early-stage.
qs: Ninety-two percent of firms have said that they have used AI at some point as part of their law practice basically.
I think that's a huge telling number, and we're still in the early innings on this.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s view that successful AI adoption depends on operational integration rather than tool access and that outside capital may intensify competition. It materially extends this by framing AI-enabled operational readiness not only as a competitive response but also as a route to scale and a potential private-equity exit, although these ownership effects are forecasts rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: And so, it's super important now for firms more than ever, that you need to be looking at the right technologies and make sure you have the right people and the right process and procedures on board, so that we can implement AI properly, and it's going to help you scale your law firm.
So maybe you become a takeover target for a PE firm, and which I think right now what this has done for law firms is a huge opportunity for buyouts.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Schmerling accepts the human-led, selective-deployment model and adds a concrete personal-injury workflow example: AI reduces medical-record review so paralegals and case managers can devote more time to client relationships. His claim that clients are not yet ready for AI-agent communication reinforces augmentation rather than wholesale substitution, although the reported business benefits are based on firm experience rather than independent causal evidence.
qs: What I've noticed in being able to help with efficiency is that allows the paralegals, the case managers, more time to communicate with clients.
And in my opinion, clients are not ready to speak to AI agents right now.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: LawPro.ai supports the proposition that LLMs make unstructured legal records tractable and that specialist value lies in a task-specific workflow layer rather than a general chatbot. Its founder-reported account does not establish accuracy, effective hallucination prevention, or a verified copilot model, but these evidentiary gaps qualify rather than contradict the cluster.
qs: But what we started noticing right off the bat was the technology was there and we're starting to make progress quickly to be able to take all these unstructured medical records and bills and structure them and be able to pull out the exact data points people are looking for.

There's about 10 to 12 different processes the medical records and bills go through in our system on the back end, including we have something called hallucination prevention technology that's patent pending right now.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI value depends on deliberate organisational integration rather than software access alone. It describes adoption as widespread but tentative, stresses strategy and workflow integration, and treats realised value as hopeful rather than demonstrated. The external-ownership discussion is speculative and attributed to the interviewer, so it does not materially alter this alignment.
qs: AI is not something you can't just go pay for AI, and your law firm changes overnight.
You have to know how you're going to use it and how you're going to integrate it.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Schmerling supports the cluster’s emphasis on organisational absorption and controlled integration rather than assuming that purchasing AI automatically transforms legal delivery. His survey evidence also reinforces the cluster’s caution that widespread experimentation and reported adoption coexist with shallow spending and early-stage implementation, although he does not directly address pricing, buyer-side reallocation or autonomous delivery.
qs: AI is not something you can't just go pay for AI, and your law firm changes overnight.
You have to know how you're going to use it and how you're going to integrate it.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of diverse competition by identifying a lawyer-built product developed within a personal injury practice and sold to other firms. Its claimed traction suggests an additional specialist entrant, but the excerpt provides no metrics or evidence about durable value, performance, market concentration or returns.
qs: And one of the interesting features of how he's been building this startup is that he's been able to build the product, but also build the product in a way where it is directly impacting the firm that he has been running while he's able to sell to other firms.
You guys obviously have some really significant traction working with some top firms.

kp.k: Medical-record automation addresses a personal injury growth bottleneck
kp.d: Schmerling says increasing case volumes made medical-record review an obstacle to his firm's growth, prompting LawPro.ai's creation. He describes large language models as enabling extraction of specific information from differently formatted, unstructured medical records and bills with substantially less engineering. The claimed benefits are faster case understanding, better decisions, increased case values and firm revenue; these are the founder's account rather than independently measured outcomes.
qs: We were getting more cases which meant more medical records for us to have to analyze and go through to help our injured clients.
Prior to large language models, you have had to do a ton of engineering to be able to pull out the information that you needed.
But really what we were trying to focus in on was how to help law firms help their clients better understand the cases faster.

kp.k: Founder describes multi-process architecture and hallucination prevention
kp.d: Schmerling distinguishes LawPro from a simple general-model wrapper, saying medical records and bills undergo approximately 10 to 12 backend processes, including patent-pending hallucination prevention technology. The transcript supplies no error rates, testing results or explanation of that prevention mechanism.
qs: There's about 10 to 12 different processes the medical records and bills go through in our system on the back end, including we have something called hallucination prevention technology that's patent pending right now.

kp.k: Practicing founder extends automation into litigation preparation
kp.d: Schmerling attributes product expansion to his own practice needs and customer feedback: beyond records, demand letters and insurance negotiations, LawPro supports discovery responses and expert-deposition preparation. He reports reducing his own preparation from hours to 15 or 20 minutes, with human cleanup remaining. Described tasks include comparing expert reports with medical records, identifying omissions or questionable conclusions, and proposing cross-examination questions; the time saving is a personal report, not a controlled comparison.
qs: We started helping with answering discovery questions.

Those depositions now, our team was able to build that out further, and those depositions now take me 15 or 20 minutes to prep for. LawPro does a lot of it, and I just do a little bit of cleanup work.
Based on that report, what's he missing from his report that should have been included based on all the medical records you're aware of?

kp.k: Different practice models require different AI workflows
kp.d: Schmerling says developing for other firms challenged his assumption that personal injury lawyers work similarly. Some settlement-oriented firms prioritize detailed 10, 20 or 30 page demands because litigation entails substantial work or referral; his firm treats the demand as a brief form document and is prepared to sue. His estimate that about half of firms share the latter approach is not tied to survey evidence. More broadly, he distinguishes pre-litigation firms, litigation specialists, referral-driven high-value practices and subject-matter niches, rejecting a one-size-fits-all market model.
qs: I thought we all practice law basically the same. And it turns out we don't. We all practice law very differently from one another.
And so some firms are really particular and want huge 10, 20, 30 page demand letters and packages.
You have personal injury firms that basically send out all their cases that need litigation, can only do pre-litigation.
And it's really interesting because it's not one size fits all.

kp.k: Continuously updated documents change the timing of legal work
kp.d: Schmerling describes Legal Docs as generating and continually updating documents when medical records and bills are uploaded, including demands customized to a firm's letterhead, structure and preferred points. Abramowitz frames this as speed enabling a new process rather than merely accelerating an existing one: a running demand draft instead of a document produced once. The host also speculates that faster discovery could support repeated testing of case theories; that is a hypothetical extension, not a reported product outcome.
qs: And so what we did is we created something called Legal Docs now, which is a document that self-generates and creates itself and continually updates itself based on the medical records that are uploaded.
But I think there's something sort of cool happening when people realize that speed is an enabler of like a new kind of like use case or a new process that you might have done.
I think we could get to a place where document discovery is something that you do like every day, multiple times a day.

kp.k: Efficiency redirects support staff toward human client relationships
kp.d: Schmerling reports that reduced record-search work gives paralegals and case managers more time for client contact. He says LawPro's Casey chatbot answers medical-record questions in five seconds and connects increased human contact with happier clients, repeat business and referrals amid rising personal injury acquisition costs. He presents clients' unwillingness to speak to AI agents as his opinion, not a measured finding; the account emphasizes redeployment rather than reported staffing cuts.
qs: What I've noticed in being able to help with efficiency is that allows the paralegals, the case managers, more time to communicate with clients.
And in my opinion, clients are not ready to speak to AI agents right now. They want to speak to humans.
We can literally ask our chatbot Casey anything we want about the medical records and we're going to have them in five seconds.
To just get repeat clients and clients referring cases to you, we have more of that coming to my law firm than ever before.

kp.k: Host links automation to upskilling rather than automatic cuts
kp.d: Abramowitz tentatively recalls an ACC CLO survey finding that 63% of surveyed chief legal officers use automation opportunities for upskilling rather than cutting. His repeated qualification that he may be mistaken matters: the transcript does not establish the exact finding or survey methodology. He argues that automation may improve or change jobs while explicitly acknowledging potential job loss.
qs: If I'm not mistaken, I think 63% of CLOs who were surveyed said that they're doing exactly that, that when they're finding places with automation, they're not using it as an opportunity to cut. They are actually using it as an opportunity to upskill.
it might take your job, it also might give you like a new and more interesting job

kp.k: Survey indicates widespread experimentation but limited AI spending
kp.d: Discussing LawPro's study with Morgan & Morgan, Schmerling says they spoke to hundreds of personal injury firms throughout the country: 92% reported having used AI at some point in practice; about 56% spent 5,000 or less currently; and about 30% spent between 5,000 and 50,000 a year. Abramowitz initially characterizes $5,000 as average spending, but Schmerling provides spending bands, not an average. The transcript gives no exact sample size or sampling methodology, and having used AI at some point is distinct from routine integration.
qs: We talked to personal injury law firms throughout the country, hundreds of personal injury law firms throughout the country, thanks to our partnership with Morgan & Morgan.
Ninety-two percent of firms have said that they have used AI at some point as part of their law practice basically.
about 56 percent of firms that we spoke to are spending 5,000 or less currently on their AI.
about 30 percent of firms from the law firms that we spoke to are spending between 5,000 and 50,000 a year in AI.

kp.k: AI adoption requires strategy and workflow integration
kp.d: Schmerling contrasts resistance when he began approaching firms about two years earlier with current acceptance. He interprets low spending as firms testing how to integrate AI and the higher-spending group as probably identifying preferred systems and integrating them into daily workflows, hopefully obtaining value. Those interpretations are qualified rather than measured survey outcomes. His recommendation is to combine technology purchasing with a strategy, appropriate people, processes and procedures.
qs: That was about two years ago that that was happening. Now, when I talk to law firms, that's gone away.
You have to have a strategy. You have to know how you're going to use it and how you're going to integrate it.

That means there's probably about 30 percent of firms have figured out which AI systems they want to use. They start really integrating into their daily workflows, and they're hopefully getting a lot of value from it.

kp.k: Private equity heightens pressure for efficient, differentiated firms
kp.d: Schmerling predicts that private equity will keep entering personal injury services, fund competitors and drive acquisition costs upward. He recommends AI-enabled efficiency, sound processes and strong client relationships as competitive responses. His firm deliberately avoids radio, television and billboards, seeking referrals and repeat clients instead of competing for those advertising channels. These are his market expectations and strategic choices, not quantified findings about private equity's effects.
qs: And my thought is that this is happening, it's going to happen, this is real, it's not going away.

what are you going to do for your law firm to make sure that you can compete as PE starts buying up some of your competitors and having more funds and more money to spend and cost of acquisition goes up.
my law firm doesn't spend anything on radio, TV, or billboards, and we're not planning on it.

kp.k: Technology becomes part of law-firm saleability
kp.d: Schmerling argues that external buyers create new exit opportunities beyond selling to partners or passing firms to children, and asserts that firm values are rising. He says prospective private-equity buyers will assess repeatable processes, operational efficiency and EBITDA, making technology relevant both to acquisition appeal and independent competitiveness. Abramowitz introduces the medical-practice MSO analogy and frames AI-first firms as prompting external-ownership discussions in 2025–2026; the transcript does not explain legal ownership restrictions or establish how any particular investment is structured.
qs: I think right now what this has done for law firms is a huge opportunity for buyouts.
So values are going up, but you have to be able to show that law firm, the PE firm, that's a repeatable process and that you have the right process of procedures.
And they're going to be looking at your EBITDA. And what's your EBITDA going to look like if you're not using real technology?
You need to start building your firm knowing that at some point, your firm either will need to get bought out by PE or you'll need to compete with PE.

kp.k: Technological change may redirect personal injury demand
kp.d: Abramowitz asks whether safer self-driving cars and harms from AI or social media will shift sources of personal injury work. Schmerling reports, with uncertain attribution to an insurer possibly Geico, a prediction that car accidents would largely end within ten years, while acknowledging the timing could be earlier or later. He anticipates other technology-related injuries and recommends monitoring emerging needs, citing social-media litigation alongside existing dog-bite and slip-and-fall work. This is speculative demand forecasting, not an established decline in accident cases.
qs: I think there was a article put out, or some kind of a paper put up by one of the insurance companies, it might have been Geico, saying that they thought that basically car accidents were going to primarily come to an end in the next 10 years.
And it could be sooner than that, could be longer than that
But there's also going to be other things happening that will be coming out as a result of all the technology that we're going through. And so you just got to keep an eye on it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Josh Schmerling claims that LawPro accelerates medical-record analysis and litigation preparation, supports continuously updated documents, increases case values, and frees staff for client service. He also presents AI adoption as a competitive and acquisition-readiness requirement for personal injury firms.
pts.d: Schmerling describes large language models as making extraction from unstructured medical records substantially faster to develop than earlier engineering approaches; his hundredfold-or-thousandfold expression is an informal estimate, not a measured productivity result. He says LawPro uses 10–12 processing stages and patent-pending hallucination-prevention technology, without supplying an error-rate claim. Specific reported capabilities include identifying omissions and errors in expert reports, suggesting cross-examination questions, assisting discovery, and producing demand letters that update as records arrive. He reports reducing his own expert-deposition preparation from hours to 15–20 minutes, with human cleanup retained. He claims faster record access allows case managers and paralegals to increase client contact, improving satisfaction and repeat/referral business, alongside higher case values. He interprets widespread experimentation but relatively limited spending as early-stage adoption. Looking ahead, he argues that AI-enabled processes can help firms scale, compete with private-equity-backed rivals, and become attractive acquisition targets.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered combines Schmerling's experience as a practitioner and product co-founder, customer feedback, and a LawPro–Morgan & Morgan survey of hundreds of personal injury firms.
pts.d: For workflow and commercial benefits, Schmerling relies on his own firm's use and reports from customers. His numerical examples are 15–20 minutes for deposition preparation and five seconds for chatbot responses about medical records. He supplies no comparative study of preparation quality, quantified case-value uplift, referral-growth figures, or measured hallucination rates. He reports that the survey found 92% had used AI at some point, about 56% spent $5,000 or less, and about 30% spent $5,000–$50,000 annually. The annual period is explicit for the latter band; the transcript does not separately specify it for the lower band. These are reported survey findings, not evidence that 92% have deeply integrated AI. His suggestion that the higher-spending group has integrated systems and receives value is explicitly tentative. The transcript does not give the exact sample size, sampling method, field dates, or questionnaire. His claims about future competition and technology's importance to acquisition attractiveness are business judgments rather than quantified forecasts.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Schmerling presents workflow benefits as already occurring, adoption as an early-stage transition over roughly two years, and competitive pressures as an ongoing development with no fixed endpoint.
pts.d: At the interview, presented as a 2026 episode, Schmerling says LawPro has existed for about two and a half years and will have been in market for two years come May. He contrasts initial skepticism with current reported AI use. Benefits depend on strategy, integration, appropriate staff and processes, and tailoring to different firms' workflows; buying software alone does not transform a practice overnight. He retains human cleanup in deposition preparation and believes clients currently prefer human communication to AI agents, qualifying substitution claims. His private-equity argument has an unspecified future horizon. On changing injury demand, he anticipates fewer car accidents and other sources of injury emerging, but the ten-year near-elimination estimate he mentions is attributed to an uncertain insurance-company source, not treated here as his own independently evidenced AI prediction.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are personal injury firms of different sizes and business models, their lawyers and support staff, injured clients, and prospective law-firm investors.
pts.d: Schmerling describes LawPro as a software provider serving personal injury firms nationwide, from solo practices to large firms, distinct from his practicing law firm. Lawyers gain faster record understanding and preparation support; paralegals and case managers shift time toward client contact rather than being described as eliminated. Injured clients are said to receive more attention and potentially higher case values. Adoption needs differ: settlement-focused firms may value lengthy, customized demand packages, whereas litigation-oriented firms such as his may not regard demand drafting as a bottleneck. Owners face decisions about growth, acquisition readiness, and competing for clients against better-funded firms; investors are described as seeking repeatable processes and attractive EBITDA. These claims concern the personal injury market, not general findings about all legal employers or access to justice.
